- Use this (not §34.4.1 "finding-grid alone") when the content has a closer that applies across all categories — e.g., a contraindication list, a wrap-up teaching, an emergency criterion.

**Example pills:** `ch2-treatment-cb1`, `ch2-treatment-cb2`.

#### 34.7.4 — Recipe: "The Deluxe — Lead + Categories + Closer" (`p + div.finding-grid + div.kb-card`)

**Frequency:** 17 pills (signature #8). This is the full canonical pattern — the one used for the most visually-rich MN pills.

**Content shape:** A topic that needs:
- A short framing paragraph at the top
- A row of 2-6 parallel categories with bullet detail in each
- A wrap-up emphatic statement at the bottom (contraindication, key teaching, summary reminder)

When all three of those elements are warranted, this is the recipe.

**Skeleton:**

```html
<article class="condition-block" id="...">
  <header class="condition-head">
    <h3 class="condition-name">{Pill Title}</h3>
    <span class="condition-tag">{Optional context tag}</span>
  </header>
  <p>{One-to-two-sentence lead — defines the topic and frames the categories below.}</p>
  <div class="finding-grid">
    <div class="finding-card">
      <h4>{Category 1}</h4>
      <ul><li>...</li></ul>
    </div>
    <div class="finding-card">
      <h4 class="flag">{Warning Category}</h4>
      <ul><li><strong>{Concerning keyword}</strong> — {explanation}</li></ul>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="kb-card">
    <p><strong>{Closing label}:</strong> {wrap-up statement applying to all categories above}</p>
  </div>
</article>
```

**Notes:**
- One of the finding-cards may use `<h4 class="flag">` to signal that the category is warning/concerning content (per §34.4.2 heading variants).
- The closing kb-card body is usually a single `<p>` with a bolded label, but may have multiple `<p>` tags or an `<h4>` + `<ul>` if the closer itself has more structure.

**When to reach for this recipe vs adjacent ones:**
- Use this (not §34.7.1 "Lead + Categories") when a closing reminder applies across all categories.
- Use this (not §34.7.3 "Categories + Closer") when the topic genuinely benefits from a framing sentence at the top.

**Example pills:** `ch1-hormonal-cb4` (Injectable progestin — the canonical reference pill: lead about IM/subQ + Timing/Long-term Concerns cards + Contraindications kb-card), `ch5-education-cb3`.

**This recipe is the visual canon's "premium" pattern.** When a pill earns this level of structure, it reads as a complete teaching module: context → details → caveats. Use sparingly — most pills don't need all three pieces.

#### 34.7.5 — Recipe: "List + Closer" (`ul + div.kb-card`)

**Frequency:** 13 pills (signature #10).

**Content shape:** A flat list of items that ends with a wrap-up reminder or contraindication. NO lead paragraph and NO categorical breakdown — the list speaks for itself, but earns a closer.

**Skeleton:**

```html
<article class="condition-block" id="...">
  <header class="condition-head">
    <h3 class="condition-name">{Pill Title}</h3>
  </header>
  <ul>
    <li>{Item 1}</li>
    <li><strong>{Key item}</strong> — {explanation}</li>
    <li>{Item 3}</li>
  </ul>
  <div class="kb-card">
    <p><strong>{Closing label}:</strong> {wrap-up}</p>
  </div>
</article>
```

**When to reach for this recipe vs adjacent ones:**
- Use this (not §34.5.1 "ul alone") when the list earns a closing emphatic note.
- Use this (not §34.7.3 "Categories + Closer") when items are flat and parallel without natural category headings.

**Example pills:** `ch10-betamethasone-cb1`, `ch11-fourth-cb2`.

#### 34.7.6 — Recipe: "Lead + Callout" (`p + div.kb-card`)

**Frequency:** 8 pills (signature #11).

**Content shape:** A topic that is essentially ONE important statement (so it lives in a kb-card), but where the title alone isn't enough framing and a one-sentence lead helps the student.

**Skeleton:**

```html
<article class="condition-block" id="...">
  <header class="condition-head">
    <h3 class="condition-name">{Pill Title}</h3>
  </header>
  <p>{One-sentence framing context.}</p>
  <div class="kb-card">
    <p><strong>{Core concept or label}:</strong> {the primary statement, often with bolded key terms}</p>
  </div>
</article>
```

**When to reach for this recipe vs adjacent ones:**
- Use this (not §34.4.3 "kb-card alone") when the standalone callout needs a sentence of context to land.
- Use this (not §34.7.1 "Lead + Categories") when the content is fundamentally one statement, not multiple categories.

**Example pills:** `ch1-natural-cb6`, `ch3-dating-cb0`.

#### 34.7.7 — Recipe: "Stacked Callouts" (`div.kb-card + div.kb-card` or 3-stack)

**Frequency:** 4 pills (signature #14) with two kb-cards; 2 pills with three kb-cards (signature in the long tail).

**Content shape:** Multiple INDEPENDENT primary statements that aren't parallel categories. Each callout stands alone but they share a chapter topic.

**Skeleton (2-stack):**

```html
<article class="condition-block" id="...">
  <header class="condition-head">
    <h3 class="condition-name">{Pill Title}</h3>
  </header>
  <div class="kb-card">
    <h4>{Concept A}</h4>
    <p>{First independent statement.}</p>
  </div>
  <div class="kb-card">
    <h4>{Concept B}</h4>
    <p>{Second independent statement.}</p>
  </div>
</article>
```

**Skeleton (3-stack — rare):** add a third `<div class="kb-card">`.

**When to reach for this recipe vs adjacent ones:**
- Use this (not §34.4.1 "finding-grid") when the items are NOT parallel categories — they're independent topics each warranting an emphatic box.
- Use this (not §34.7.4 "Deluxe") when there's no overarching framing paragraph or wrap-up.

**Distinguishing test:** "Could these be presented as parallel sub-headings (Cause vs Symptom vs Treatment, or A vs B vs C)?" If yes → finding-grid recipe. If no → stacked kb-cards.

**Example pills:** `ch14-als-cb1`, `ch23-classification-cb3`.

#### 34.7.8 — Recipe: "The Answer Key Pattern" (`div.kb-card + div.finding-grid + span.nclex-tag`)

**Frequency:** 6 pills (signature #12). Used SPECIFICALLY on Answer Key / exemplar / high-yield concept pills — never on regular content pills.

**Content shape:** An exemplar pill that:
1. Opens with the **underlying concept or rationale** as an emphatic primary statement (kb-card with `<h4>` heading like "Underlying Principles — {Concept Name}")
2. Shows **practical applications** in a row of categorical cards (the strategies, interventions, or sub-types that flow from the concept)
3. Ends with an **NCLEX category footer label** mapping the pill to specific test categories

**Skeleton:**

```html
<article class="condition-block" id="...">
  <header class="condition-head">
    <h3 class="condition-name">Answer key</h3>
  </header>
  <div class="kb-card">
    <h4>Underlying Principles — {Concept Name}</h4>
    <p>{The principle / rationale being explained, in primary-statement prose.}</p>
  </div>
  <div class="finding-grid">
    <div class="finding-card">
      <h4>{Application Category 1}</h4>
      <ul><li>...</li></ul>
    </div>
    <div class="finding-card">
      <h4>{Application Category 2}</h4>
      <ul><li>...</li></ul>
    </div>
  </div>
  <span class="nclex-tag">NCLEX · {Test Category} · {Sub-category}</span>
</article>
```

**Pill title convention:** Answer Key pills typically have `<h3 class="condition-name">Answer key</h3>` as the title. Sometimes a specific exemplar gets a different title (e.g., "Underlying principles — Gate-control theory of pain"); both are valid.

**When to reach for this recipe:**
- ONLY on Answer Key / exemplar / NCLEX-prep pills. Do NOT use the nclex-tag on regular content pills (§34.6.2 rule).
- The kb-card-first structure (vs the more common p-first structure) is intentional — it signals that the OPENING content is the primary teaching point, not a setup paragraph.

**Example pills:** `ch12-als-cb1` (gate-control theory of pain → sensory & cutaneous strategies), `ch15-als-cb1`.

### 34.7.9 — The long tail (rare and one-off compositions)

Phase A found 32 unique signatures that cover only 17 pills (2.8% of MN). These are one-off variations — pills where the author needed a structure that didn't quite fit any of the 8 recipes above. Examples:

- `p + div.finding-grid + div.finding-grid + div.kb-card` (2 pills) — two finding-grids stacked, then a closer
- `p + ul + div.kb-card` (2 pills) — lead + list + closer
- `p + table.data-table + div.kb-card` (1 pill) — lead + table + closer
- `p + div.kb-card + p + p` (1 pill) — lead + callout + trailing prose

**Rule for the long tail:** These exist; they are valid in their specific pills; they should not be treated as new recipes. When composing a new pill, prefer one of the 8 named recipes (§34.7.1-§34.7.8). Only stray into long-tail territory when the content genuinely cannot be expressed in a named recipe — and document that decision in a comment for future review.

**Possible canon-violators in the long tail:** A small number of the long-tail pills may actually be the same kind of "wrong wrapper" mistake as Batch E. Phase F (forbidden patterns) will list any long-tail signatures that should be refactored to a named recipe. For now, the long tail is not actively audited.

### 34.7.10 — Master decision table (refreshed with all recipes)

Consolidated table covering every documented pattern. When composing a new pill, scan this table top-to-bottom for the FIRST content-shape row that matches your content:

| Content shape | Recipe / Block | Section | Pill count |
|---|---|---|---|
| **One short statement / referral** | `<div class="kb-card">` alone | §34.4.3 | 34 |
| **One short statement with brief lead** | `p + kb-card` (Recipe 6) | §34.7.6 | 8 |
| **Flat list of items** | `<ul>` alone | §34.5.1 | 172 |
| **Flat list of warning signs / red flags** | `<ul class="flag-list">` alone | §34.5.3 | 37 |
| **Numbered procedural sequence** | `<ol>` alone | §34.5.2 | 4 |
| **Flat list with brief lead** | `p + ul` (Recipe 2) | §34.7.2 | 22 |
| **Flat list ending with a wrap-up** | `ul + kb-card` (Recipe 5) | §34.7.5 | 13 |
| **2-6 parallel categories** | `<div class="finding-grid">` alone | §34.4.1 | 160 |
| **2-6 parallel categories with brief lead** | `p + finding-grid` (Recipe 1) | §34.7.1 | 43 |
| **2-6 parallel categories with wrap-up closer** | `finding-grid + kb-card` (Recipe 3) | §34.7.3 | 17 |
| **2-6 parallel categories with lead and closer** | `p + finding-grid + kb-card` (Recipe 4 / Deluxe) | §34.7.4 | 17 |
| **Multiple INDEPENDENT primary statements** | `kb-card + kb-card` (Recipe 7) | §34.7.7 | 4-6 |
| **Side-by-side comparison data** | `<table class="data-table">` alone | §34.6.1 | 6 |
| **Answer Key / exemplar / NCLEX-prep pill** | `kb-card + finding-grid + nclex-tag` (Recipe 8 / Answer Key) | §34.7.8 | 6 |
| **One-off composition not matching any above** | LONG TAIL — document decision | §34.7.9 | 17 |
| **FORBIDDEN: bare paragraph alone** | `<p>` alone | §34.5.4 | 22 (slated for refactor) |
| **FORBIDDEN: kb-card as primary multi-category container** | `kb-card` with mega-`<ul>` | §34.4.5 | 4 PD pills (slated for refactor) |

**Decision rule of thumb:**
1. Start by classifying the content's natural SHAPE in one word: "list," "categories," "statement," "table," "exemplar," "stacked."
2. Then ask: "Does it need a lead?" "Does it need a closer?" "Is it a warning?"
3. The combination of answers maps to ONE row of the table. Pick that recipe.

If two recipes seem to fit, prefer the more frequent one (the recipe with more pill count in MN) — that's the more canonical choice.


### 34.8 — Phase D: Header / pill-shell catalog

Phases B and C documented the body content (blocks and compositions). This phase documents the SHELL — the outer wrapper and header structure that every MN pill shares regardless of body recipe. The shell is invariant; the recipe is what varies.

#### 34.8.1 — `<article class="condition-block">` (the outer pill shell)

**Purpose:** The outer container for a single pill. Every pill is exactly one `<article class="condition-block">` element. This is the fundamental atomic unit of MN's content (and PD/Pharm/MH's content).

**Tag/class:** `<article class="condition-block" id="ch{N}-{section}-{cb-id}">`

**ID convention:** `ch{N}-{section-id}-{cb-id}` where:
- `{N}` is the chapter number (1-27 for MN)
- `{section-id}` is the parent `<section class="content-section">`'s id minus the `ch{N}-` prefix
- `{cb-id}` is one of `cb0`, `cb1`, `cb2`, … (a sequential counter) OR a semantic suffix like `-h0`, `-h1` (used for header-style overview pills in PD and Pharm)

Example: `<article class="condition-block" id="ch1-hormonal-cb4">` — chapter 1, section "hormonal" (inside section `ch1-hormonal`), 5th pill (zero-indexed).

**CSS** (from MN Book file — shared with `.kb-card`):

```css
.condition-block,
.kb-card {
  background: var(--surface);
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: 14px;
  padding: 20px 22px;
  margin: 0 0 28px;
  position: relative;
  transition: border-color .15s ease;
}
.condition-block:hover,
.kb-card:hover {
  border-color: var(--text3);
}
.condition-block.pill-flash {
  animation: pillFlash 1.8s ease-out;
  border-radius: 8px;
}
```

**Note on the shared CSS:** The outer pill shell (`condition-block`) and the inner emphatic callout (`kb-card`) share the same box styling. The kb-card is essentially "a condition-block-sized box used as an inner element." This is a deliberate design choice — the same visual treatment applies at two scales. Future-Claude does not need to re-style either; both are styled once via the shared selector.

**Special class:** `.pill-flash` (added briefly via JS when the user navigates to a pill from a search result or sidebar link) — provides a 1.8-second flash animation to highlight which pill the user landed on. This is dynamic and does not need to be authored.

**JavaScript-inserted children:** The book's bookmark-button JS inserts a `<button class="pill-bookmark-btn">` into each `<header class="condition-head">` at runtime. Future-Claude does NOT include this button in authored HTML — the JS adds it on page load. Mentioned here so authored HTML matches what's expected (header has at most a `<h3>` and an optional `<span class="condition-tag">`; everything else is JS-managed).

**Children** (canonical order):
1. REQUIRED `<header class="condition-head">` (§34.8.2)
2. OPTIONAL body content per the recipes in §34.7 (or single-block patterns from §34.4-§34.6)

**Skeleton (empty shell):**

```html
<article class="condition-block" id="ch{N}-{section}-{cb-id}">
  <header class="condition-head">
    <h3 class="condition-name">{Pill Title}</h3>
    <!-- optional <span class="condition-tag">{tag}</span> -->
  </header>
  <!-- body content per chosen recipe from §34.7 -->
</article>
```

#### 34.8.2 — `<header class="condition-head">` (the pill header bar)

**Purpose:** Holds the title and optional contextual tag side-by-side at the top of the pill, separated from the body by a bottom border. Acts as a visual division — what comes above is the pill's identification; what comes below is its content.

**Tag/class:** `<header class="condition-head">`

**CSS** (from MN Book file):

```css
.condition-head {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-items: baseline;
  gap: 10px 14px;
  margin: 0 0 12px;
  padding-bottom: 10px;
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-soft);
}
```

**Visual behavior:** A flexbox container. Title sits as the primary item (flex:1 from its own CSS); tag (if present) wraps to the right at the baseline. 10px row-gap, 14px column-gap. 12px bottom margin separates header from body. Has a 1px bottom border in `--border-soft` (very subtle line under the title).

**Children:**
1. REQUIRED `<h3 class="condition-name">{Title}</h3>` (§34.8.3)
2. OPTIONAL `<span class="condition-tag">{Tag content}</span>` (§34.8.4)
3. The JS-inserted `<button class="pill-bookmark-btn">` (added at runtime; not authored)

**Skeleton:**

```html
<header class="condition-head">
  <h3 class="condition-name">{Pill Title}</h3>
  <span class="condition-tag">{Optional one-line context}</span>
</header>
```

**Skeleton without tag** (most common case — 549 of 610 pills have no tag):

```html
<header class="condition-head">
  <h3 class="condition-name">{Pill Title}</h3>
</header>
```

#### 34.8.3 — `<h3 class="condition-name">` (the pill title)

**Purpose:** The pill's name. Always exactly one per pill. Acts as the heading-level entry point — appears as the bold serif title at the top of every pill, AND is the text that appears in chapter-modal sidebars and search results.

**Tag/class:** `<h3 class="condition-name">`

**CSS** (from MN Book file):

```css
.condition-name {
  font-family: 'DM Serif Display', serif;
  font-weight: 400;
  font-size: 20px;
  line-height: 1.25;
  color: var(--text);
  margin: 0;
  flex: 1;
  min-width: 200px;
}
.condition-name.flag,
.kb-card h3.flag,
.kb-card h4.flag {
  position: relative;
  padding-left: 14px;
}
.condition-name.flag::before,
.kb-card h3.flag::before,
.kb-card h4.flag::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  left: 0;
  top: 50%;
  transform: translateY(-50%);
  width: 4px;
  height: 70%;
  background: var(--nonreassuring);
  border-radius: 2px;
}
```

**Visual behavior:** Serif font (DM Serif Display), 20px, normal weight (400 — not bold; the serif gives weight visually), full-brightness text. Takes flex:1 (grows to fill available space). 200px minimum width ensures it doesn't get squeezed on narrow screens when a long tag is present.

**Variant: `<h3 class="condition-name flag">`** — adds a red-coral vertical bar (4px wide, 70% height) on the LEFT side of the title, padding the text 14px to the right. Used when the entire pill is about WARNING content — distinct from `condition-tag flag` (which adds the bar to a tag), this puts the bar on the title itself.

**When to use `.condition-name.flag`:**
- The pill's primary content IS the warning (not just one section of it). Examples might be "Postpartum hemorrhage warning signs", "Severe preeclampsia criteria", "Emergency cesarean indications."
- Avoid using `condition-name.flag` on pills that already use `<ul class="flag-list">` as their body — that would double-flag the visual. Pick ONE flag location (title OR list) per pill.

**Content guidelines for the title:**
- Match the source material's heading. Don't editorialize.
- Use sentence case for prose-style titles ("Injectable progestin (medroxyprogesterone / Depo-Provera)") OR title case for noun-form titles ("Postpartum Hemorrhage") — match adjacent pills' convention within the section.
- Avoid trailing punctuation.
- Generic titles like "Findings" or "Nursing care" are acceptable when the parent section provides context (`<section id="ch10-preterm" class="content-section"><h2>Preterm labor</h2>...<article id="ch10-preterm-cb1"><h3 class="condition-name">Findings</h3>` — the section heading "Preterm labor" makes "Findings" specific enough).

#### 34.8.4 — `<span class="condition-tag">` (the optional contextual label)

**Purpose:** A small uppercase accent-colored label next to the title that adds ONE line of context too specific for the title but too useful to bury in the body. Acts like a "subtitle" or "key qualifier."

**Tag/class:** `<span class="condition-tag">` (bare) or `<span class="condition-tag flag">` (with flag modifier)

**CSS** (from MN Book file):

```css
.condition-tag {
  font-size: 11px;
  font-weight: 600;
  color: var(--accent2);
  background: var(--accent-soft);
  padding: 4px 10px;
  border-radius: 6px;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
  white-space: nowrap;
}
```

(The `condition-tag flag` variant adds the red-coral vertical bar via the shared `.flag::before` rule documented in §34.4.2.)

**Visual behavior:** A small rounded-corner label (6px radius). Background in `--accent-soft` (a low-opacity tint of the book's accent color). Text in `--accent2` (the book's accent — amber for MN, sky for PD, etc.). ALL CAPS, 11px, slightly letter-spaced. `white-space: nowrap` keeps multi-word tags from wrapping mid-tag (so "Most effective method of birth control" stays on one line).

**Frequency:** 61 occurrences across 610 pills — about 10% of pills carry a tag. The other 90% are tag-free.

**Content patterns (7 categories, by frequency of appearance):**

Tag content falls into seven canonical patterns. Use this as a glossary when deciding what tag to add (if any) to a new pill:

| Pattern | Example values | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanism / key descriptor** | "Estrogen + progestin", "LARC", "Estrogen/progesterone-driven" | When the pill's mechanism is its defining feature and the title doesn't say it |
| **Severity / rank** | "Most effective method of birth control", "Least effective", "Leading bleeding-related cause of maternal death (1st trimester)" | When the pill represents an extreme on a scale and that ranking is the key takeaway |
| **Type / nature** | "ART-associated", "Hyperpigmentation", "Subjective · client experiences", "Objective · examiner finds" | When the pill is one of several parallel types in the section and the type IS the qualifier |
| **Warning indicator** (use with `flag`) | "Red flags", "Critical · neural tube defects" | When the pill's primary content is warning material — pair with `<ul class="flag-list">` body OR the `.flag` class on title |
| **Test focus** | "High-yield NCLEX", "High-yield NCLEX cues" | When the pill is flagged as exam-prep priority (sparingly — 3 of 61 tags use this) |
| **Action prompt** | "Identify candidates early", "Support, educate, refer", "Assess every visit", "Judgment-free support" | When the pill's takeaway is what the nurse should DO (an actionable orientation) |
| **Numerical / specific** | "Rho(D) ~28 wk if Rh-negative", "<3/hr or none ×12 hr → notify" | When the pill's most important takeaway is a specific number or threshold |

**Rule for using a tag:**
- The tag must add information not present in the title.
- Use sparingly — most pills (90%) don't need one. If you can't decide, default to no tag.
- One tag per pill. Multiple tags are not supported by the layout.
- Use uppercase or sentence case in the source text; CSS handles the visual `text-transform: uppercase`. Either is fine — but sentence case is easier to author.

**Skeleton (bare tag):**

```html
<header class="condition-head">
  <h3 class="condition-name">{Pill Title}</h3>
  <span class="condition-tag">{One-line context}</span>
</header>
```

**Skeleton (flag tag — warning):**

```html
<header class="condition-head">
  <h3 class="condition-name">{Pill Title}</h3>
  <span class="condition-tag flag">{Warning label}</span>
</header>
```

#### 34.8.5 — Header conventions: title + tag pairing

Some pairing rules for title and tag together:

- **Title says WHAT; tag says WHY or HOW SEVERE.** Title: "Injectable progestin (medroxyprogesterone / Depo-Provera)". Tag: implicit — the pill body explains it's a hormonal LARC alternative. (This pill happens to have no tag; the body is rich enough.)
- **Title says WHAT; tag says WHEN or WHICH.** Title: "Skin changes". Tag: "Hyperpigmentation" — narrows the WHAT down to a specific TYPE.
- **Title says GENERIC SECTION ROLE; tag adds SPECIFICITY.** Title: "Report immediately". Tag: "Red flags". Together: this pill is the warning-signs section.
- **Title says CONCEPT; tag says ACTION.** Title: "Adoption considerations". Tag: "Judgment-free support" (clinician action). Together: the pill's takeaway is HOW to act.

These pairings are not enforced by code — they are editorial guidelines. Apply when authoring.

#### 34.8.6 — Complete pill shell skeleton

The canonical bare skeleton every new pill starts as, before any recipe is applied to the body:

```html
<article class="condition-block" id="ch{N}-{section}-{cb-id}">
  <header class="condition-head">
    <h3 class="condition-name">{Pill Title}</h3>
    <!-- Add this line only if a contextual tag adds value:
    <span class="condition-tag">{One-line context}</span>
    -->
  </header>
  <!-- Body content goes here. Look up the matching recipe in §34.7.10 (master decision table)
       based on content shape, then expand the skeleton from the recipe section (§34.4 to §34.7). -->
</article>
```

After this shell is written, the body content is filled in by:
1. Identifying the content's natural SHAPE.
2. Looking up the matching recipe in the master decision table (§34.7.10).
3. Copying that recipe's skeleton (§34.4 - §34.7) into the body.
4. Replacing `{placeholders}` with actual content.
5. Verifying the resulting pill against the recipe's example pills (spot-check on live site).

#### 34.8.7 — Cross-references

- The `condition-block` outer shell's CSS is documented again in this section for completeness; it's also referenced in §34.4.3 because `.kb-card` shares the same CSS rule.
- The `.flag` class on `<h3 class="condition-name">` and `<h4>` headings (inside finding-card and kb-card) uses the same red-coral vertical bar — documented per-element in §34.4.2 (finding-card h4), §34.4.3 (kb-card h4), and here for condition-name. The visual treatment is identical across all three contexts.
- Future-Claude composing a NEW pill: start with §34.8.6 (shell skeleton), then jump to §34.7.10 (decision table) to pick a body recipe.


### 34.9 — Phase E: Modifier class catalog

Modifier classes are CSS classes that ALTER the rendering of an underlying element without changing its structural role. They're additive — applied alongside the element's primary class to layer a treatment on top. This phase consolidates all canonical modifier classes used in MN's pill-related content.

**Definition (for this catalog):** A modifier class is one that:
1. Has fewer than 10 rule mentions in the CSS (small-scope CSS footprint).
2. Is applied via `class="primary-class modifier"` syntax (combined, not standalone).
3. Adjusts color, accent, padding, or text alignment without changing the element's structural meaning.

Modifiers we have already encountered (and consolidate here) plus newly-identified ones:

#### 34.9.1 — `.flag` (the canonical warning modifier — CONSOLIDATED)

**Purpose:** Marks an element as containing or representing WARNING content. Visually signals concern by adding a red-coral (`--nonreassuring` #e05c6a) accent — either a vertical bar to the LEFT of inline elements or a left-side border accent on block elements.

**Tag/class:** modifier class — `<{element} class="{primary-class} flag">` (combined)

**CSS** (consolidated from MN Book file — all 5 rules involving `.flag`):

```css
/* Brief-card heading variant */
.brief-grid h3.flag {
  color: var(--nonreassuring);
}

/* flag-list bullet marker (specific to brief-grid context) */
.brief-grid .flag-list li::before {
  background: var(--nonreassuring);
}

/* List-level flag: changes border + adds vertical bar on the LEFT of the list box */
.condition-block > ul.flag-list,
.condition-block > ol.flag-list,
.content-section > ul.flag-list,
.content-section > ol.flag-list {
  border-color: var(--nonreassuring);
  background: linear-gradient(0deg, rgba(0,0,0,0) 0%, rgba(0,0,0,0) 100%), var(--surface2);
  box-shadow: inset 3px 0 0 var(--nonreassuring);
}

/* Heading/title-level flag: adds vertical bar to the LEFT of the text */
.condition-name.flag,
.kb-card h3.flag,
.kb-card h4.flag {
  position: relative;
  padding-left: 14px;
}
.condition-name.flag::before,
.kb-card h3.flag::before,
.kb-card h4.flag::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  left: 0;
  top: 50%;
  transform: translateY(-50%);
  width: 4px;
  height: 70%;
  background: var(--nonreassuring);
  border-radius: 2px;
}
```

**Visual treatments by application context:**

| Context | Markup | Visual result |
|---|---|---|
| Pill title | `<h3 class="condition-name flag">` | Red-coral vertical bar (4px wide, 70% height) before the title text, padded 14px right |
| finding-card heading | `<h4 class="flag">` (inside `.finding-card`) | (Inherits the heading rule via the shared `.kb-card h4.flag` selector — but ONLY works inside a kb-card per the selector; finding-card needs separate documentation — see note below) |
| kb-card heading | `<h4 class="flag">` (inside `.kb-card`) | Red-coral vertical bar before the heading text |
| kb-card subheading | `<h3 class="flag">` (inside `.kb-card`) | Red-coral vertical bar before the subheading text |
| Header tag | `<span class="condition-tag flag">` | Adds the same vertical-bar treatment via the shared rule |
| List (ul/ol) | `<ul class="flag-list">` or `<ol class="flag-list">` | Changes the box's border color to red-coral and adds a 3px inset box-shadow on the LEFT (visual analog to the bar) |

**Important inconsistency to fix in future work:** The current CSS selector for the heading bar is `.condition-name.flag, .kb-card h3.flag, .kb-card h4.flag` — it does NOT include `.finding-card h4.flag`. This means a `<h4 class="flag">` inside a finding-card is partially unstyled (the color is fine via the standard `.finding-card h4` rule, but the bar accent does not appear). The user's screenshot example `ch1-hormonal-cb4` shows `<h4 class="flag">Long-term concerns</h4>` inside a finding-card — review whether the bar accent renders in practice or if this is a latent CSS gap. If the bar is missing for finding-card h4.flag, this is a CSS bug to track separately (NOT a modifier-doc issue). Flagged here for future investigation.

**RESOLVED 2026-05-31:** Investigation confirmed both color AND specificity issues:
- The `.finding-card h4` rule (color: `var(--accent2)`) was winning the cascade over the base `.flag` rule (color: `var(--nonreassuring)`) due to specificity (0,1,1) vs (0,1,0)
- 40 h4.flag elements in MN finding-cards were rendering in amber instead of red-coral
- Fix: added explicit `.finding-card h4.flag` rule to all 4 Books (MN/PD/MH/Pharm) with `color: var(--nonreassuring); position: relative; padding-left: 14px;` — specificity (0,2,1) overrides both
- All 4 Books updated for consistency; only MN currently uses this combination but PD/MH/Pharm CSS is the shared framework
- Bar accent (`.flag::before`) was always working — only the color was the issue

**Decision rule — when to use `.flag`:**

1. The element represents WARNING content (red flags, contraindications, critical findings, "report immediately" items, severe complications).
2. Pick ONE flag context per pill — don't double-flag.
   - If using `<ul class="flag-list">` as the body, don't also flag the title.
   - If using `<h3 class="condition-name flag">`, don't also use a flag-list body.
   - The signal should land in ONE place to remain clear.
3. The flag class is the visual analog of using "warning" or "alert" in spoken language — apply sparingly so it retains meaning when present.

#### 34.9.2 — `.severity` (the 3-level severity badge)

**Purpose:** A standalone inline-block badge labeling content with one of three severity levels. Used as a small pill-shaped indicator with a colored dot. Currently used in MN exclusively on FHR (Fetal Heart Rate) pattern classification headers, but the markup is general-purpose for any 3-level severity scale.

**Tag/class:** `<span class="severity {variant}">{Label text}</span>` where `{variant}` is one of `reassuring`, `concerning`, `critical`.

**CSS** (from MN Book file):

```css
.severity {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 6px;
  font-size: 10.5px;
  font-weight: 700;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  letter-spacing: 0.14em;
  padding: 4px 10px;
  border-radius: 4px;
  flex-shrink: 0;
}
.severity.reassuring {
  background: var(--reassuring-bg);
  color: var(--reassuring);
}
.severity.concerning {
  background: var(--indeterminate-bg);
  color: var(--indeterminate);
}
.severity.critical {
  background: var(--nonreassuring-bg);
  color: var(--nonreassuring);
}
.severity::before {
  content: '';
  width: 6px;
  height: 6px;
  border-radius: 50%;
  background: currentColor;
}
```

**Color palette:**

| Variant | Color variable | Hex | Background (`-bg`) | Semantics |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `reassuring` | `--reassuring` | `#3db87a` (green) | `rgba(61,184,122,0.10)` | Normal, non-emergency, expected |
| `concerning` | `--indeterminate` | `#e8a838` (amber) | `rgba(232,168,56,0.10)` | Intermediate, watch closely |
| `critical` | `--nonreassuring` | `#e05c6a` (red-coral) | `rgba(224,92,106,0.10)` | Urgent, non-reassuring, requires action |

Note that the `concerning` variant uses the `--indeterminate` variable (not `--concerning`) — the variant NAME and the CSS variable NAME differ by intent. "Concerning" is the user-facing label; "indeterminate" is the underlying clinical-classification term (matches the NCCC FHR Category II indeterminate findings).

**Visual behavior:** A small pill-shaped badge (4px corners). A 6px colored dot precedes the text (matches the text color via `currentColor`). Text is tiny (10.5px) ALL-CAPS, bold (700), letter-spaced 0.14em. Background is a 10% tint of the foreground color. `flex-shrink: 0` keeps it from compressing inside flex containers.

**Frequency:** 7 occurrences in MN — exclusively on FHR pattern headers inside `<header>` elements of specialty pattern cards (e.g., Accelerations / Fetal bradycardia / Fetal tachycardia / Variability / Decelerations).

**Label text rule:** The label text inside the span is contextual, not fixed to the class name. The CSS class determines color and dot; the text determines the description. So:
- `severity reassuring` may carry text "Reassuring" OR "Benign" (both render green)
- `severity concerning` carries text "Concerning"
- `severity critical` may carry text "Concerning" OR "Critical" (both render red — the label "Concerning" on a critical class signals "this looks concerning AND is critical")

This text-class pairing is intentional editorial flexibility. When authoring NEW content using `.severity`, choose:
1. The CLASS based on the actual severity level (reassuring = green, concerning = amber, critical = red).
2. The TEXT based on what the source material calls the finding.

**Skeleton:**

```html
<span class="severity reassuring">Reassuring</span>
<span class="severity concerning">Concerning</span>
<span class="severity critical">Critical</span>
```

**Use case in context (where `.severity` actually appears in MN):**

Inside a specialty `pattern-card` block (not yet catalogued; see §34.9.5 for note about non-pill block scope). The card header has the pattern name + a `.severity` badge:

```html
<div class="pattern-card">
  <header class="pattern-card-header">
    <h3>Fetal tachycardia</h3>
    <span class="severity concerning">Concerning</span>
  </header>
  <p class="pattern-defn">...</p>
  ...
</div>
```

**Do not** use `.severity` inside `.finding-card` or `.kb-card` headings — those use `.flag` (§34.9.1) for warning treatment, not the 3-level severity badge. The two systems are visually distinct and not interchangeable: `.flag` is a binary warning marker (warning or not); `.severity` is a graded severity classifier (reassuring / concerning / critical).

#### 34.9.3 — Data-table modifiers (consolidated)

The `<table class="data-table">` block supports several modifier classes. All are documented in detail in §34.6.1; consolidated here as a reference.

**Modifier classes applicable to `.data-table`:**

| Modifier | Applies to | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `.compact` | `<table class="data-table compact">` | Reduces table font-size to 13px and cell padding to 8×12 (for dense tables) |
| `.score-0` | `<td>` or `<span>` inside data-table cell | Red text (#dc2626), weight 600 — for critical/0-point scores |
| `.score-1` | same | Amber text (#d97706), weight 600 — for intermediate/1-point scores |
| `.score-2` | same | Green text (#059669), weight 600 — for normal/2-point scores |
| `.col-center` | `<th>` or `<td>` | Center-align text in the column |
| `.col-num` | `<th>` or `<td>` | Right-align text + tabular numeric figures (for number columns) |
| `.row-header` | `<td>` (typically the leftmost cell of a row) | Renders the cell as a label-style row header — bold, full-brightness text, surface2 background |

**Usage example** (Apgar scoring or similar 0/1/2 scoring table — see §34.6.1 skeleton):

```html
<table class="data-table">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Sign</th>
      <th class="col-center">0 points</th>
      <th class="col-center">1 point</th>
      <th class="col-center">2 points</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td class="row-header">Heart rate</td>
      <td class="col-center"><span class="score-0">Absent</span></td>
      <td class="col-center"><span class="score-1">&lt;100/min</span></td>
      <td class="col-center"><span class="score-2">&gt;100/min</span></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
```

**Note:** The `.compact` modifier is rarely used; default `.data-table` sizing is appropriate for most tables. Use `.compact` only when 4+ columns make the default sizing crowded.

#### 34.9.4 — General modifier rules

These rules govern all modifier classes, not just the ones documented above:

1. **Don't invent new modifier classes.** The CSS does not auto-style classes that don't have a rule. A `<h4 class="warning">` or `<span class="kb-tag">` will appear unstyled (this is exactly the Batch E mistake — see §34.4.5). If you need a new visual treatment that isn't documented here, escalate to add the class + CSS first, then use it. Do not author with imagined classes.

2. **Apply modifiers only in their documented contexts.** Most modifiers are scoped (e.g., `.score-0` only works inside `.data-table` cells; `.severity` works as a standalone `<span>` but not as a heading; `.flag` works on certain headings, lists, and tags but not on arbitrary elements). The CSS selectors enforce these scopes — applying outside the scope yields no styling.

3. **One flag location per pill** (specific to `.flag`). If using `<ul class="flag-list">`, do not also use `<h3 class="condition-name flag">`. The signal should land in exactly one place.

4. **`.severity` is graded; `.flag` is binary.** They are not interchangeable. Use `.severity` for content fitting a 3-level severity scale (typically FHR or clinical-classification systems). Use `.flag` for content that is generically WARNING in nature regardless of grading.

5. **Modifier text content matches the modifier semantic.** For `.severity`, the label text should match the class (or a synonym): "Reassuring"/"Benign" with `severity reassuring`, "Concerning" with `severity concerning`, "Concerning"/"Critical" with `severity critical`. For `.flag`, no specific text constraint — the class adds the visual; the text is whatever the source calls it.

#### 34.9.5 — Out-of-scope: non-pill structural blocks

The catalog as built (Phases A through G — coverage of `<article class="condition-block">` content) is intentionally scoped to PILL CONTENT. MN's design vocabulary extends beyond pill bodies into several additional structural block types that this catalog does NOT currently document. They are listed here so future-Claude is aware of their existence and does not mistakenly treat them as undefined territory:

| Block class | CSS rule count | Apparent use |
|---|---|---|
| `.exercise` | 57 rules | NCLEX practice question blocks (full Q/A/rationale structure with reveal interaction) |
| `.modal` | 36 rules | Chapter modal overlay infrastructure |
| `.sidebar` | 29 rules | Side navigation infrastructure |
| `.mid-read` / `.mid-prompt` | 28+27 rules | Self-check quick-recall questions inserted between pills mid-chapter |
| `.als-card` | 17 rules | Active Learning Strategy summary cards |
| `.tier-card` | 16 rules | Tier-based comparison cards |
| `.concept-card` | 13 rules | Concept summary cards |
| `.callout` | 12 rules | Generic callout boxes (different from kb-card) |
| `.pattern-card` | 8 rules | FHR pattern cards (uses `.severity`) |
| `.trimester-card`, `.split-card`, `.brief-grid`, `.brief-banner` | 4-8 rules each | Specialty visual cards |

**Scope decision:** Cataloging these is future work (potential "Phase I — Non-pill structural blocks"). The current PART 34 ends with Phase H (handoff). Cataloging the non-pill blocks would require a similar inventory-and-document approach as Phase A-D applied to pill bodies. This is a substantial effort and is deferred.

**Rule for future-Claude in the interim:** When authoring NEW non-pill content (e.g., writing a new exercise block, a new pattern card, a new mid-read), DO NOT invent structural classes. Find an existing usage in MN, view its HTML, and replicate that structure faithfully. The classes are already in MN's CSS; the patterns just aren't catalogued yet here.


### 34.10 — Phase F: Forbidden patterns catalog (anti-patterns)

This section consolidates every anti-pattern identified across the catalog into one reference. Future-Claude reading PART 34 for the first time should read THIS SECTION FIRST — it documents what NOT to do, then point to §34.7.10 (decision table) for what to do instead.

**General principle:** MN's visual canon is finite and complete. Every content shape encountered has a canonical pattern in §34.4–§34.7. If a content shape seems not to fit any pattern, that is a signal to (a) re-examine the content shape (it may match a recipe you missed), or (b) flag for human review — NOT a license to invent a new pattern.

The 10 forbidden patterns and anti-patterns:

#### 34.10.1 — Bare `<p>` alone as pill body (FORBIDDEN)

**Pattern:**

```html
<article class="condition-block" id="...">
  <header class="condition-head">
    <h3 class="condition-name">Pill Title</h3>
  </header>
  <p>Just a paragraph and nothing else.</p>
</article>
```

**Why forbidden:** Every pill body MUST contain at least one boxed inner element. A bare paragraph lacks any "pill inside the pill" treatment — the §32 canon rule, formalized in §34.4.4 and §34.5.4.

**Current violators in the suite** (May 30, 2026):
- 22 pills in MN (signature #6 in §34.3 — exact pill IDs catalogued in §34.5.4 listing)
- 13 pills in PD
- 5 pills in MH
- 0 pills in Pharm

**Total:** 40 pills suite-wide pending refactor.

**Refactor rule:** Apply §34.5.4's refactor pipeline based on the paragraph's content shape:
- If the paragraph defines a single concept → convert to `p + kb-card` (§34.7.6)
- If the paragraph describes 2-6 facets → convert to `p + finding-grid` (§34.7.1) or "Deluxe" (§34.7.4)
- If the paragraph lists warning signs in prose → convert to `p + ul.flag-list` or similar

#### 34.10.2 — `<span class="kb-tag">` (FORBIDDEN — invented class)

**Pattern:**

```html
<div class="kb-card">
  <span class="kb-tag">SOME LABEL TEXT</span>
  ...
</div>
```

**Why forbidden:** `.kb-tag` has NO CSS rule defined anywhere in the 4 books' CSS files. The class renders as completely unstyled inline text. This class was invented during Batch E (May 30, 2026) as an attempt to add an accent label inside a kb-card — but no such mechanism exists in the canonical design.

**The correct mechanism:** kb-card supports `<h4>` (optionally `<h4 class="flag">`) for accent-colored headings — see §34.4.3. If a kb-card needs a label, use the `<h4>` heading, not an invented tag class.

**Status:** This pattern appears in 4 PD pills authored in Batch E (the 4 PD empty pills that got enriched). All 4 are slated for refactor — see §34.10.3 below.

#### 34.10.3 — `<div class="kb-card">` as primary multi-category container (ANTI-PATTERN)

**Pattern:**

```html
<p>Lead paragraph...</p>
<div class="kb-card">
  <span class="kb-tag">CATEGORIES</span>   <!-- also forbidden per §34.10.2 -->
  <h4>Mega-heading</h4>
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Category 1</strong> — description</li>
    <li><strong>Category 2</strong> — description</li>
    <li><strong>Category 3</strong> — description</li>
    <li><strong>Category 4</strong> — description</li>
  </ul>
</div>
```

**Why anti-pattern:** When content has 2-6 parallel categories of equal weight, the canonical container is `<div class="finding-grid">` with multiple `<div class="finding-card">` children — see §34.4.4 row 3. Using `kb-card` for this purpose:
- Loses the per-category accent-color heading (each finding-card has its own `<h4>` in `--accent2`; the mega-list inside kb-card has only ONE heading)
- Loses the visual separation between categories (they're flat bullets in one box, not distinct cards)
- Uses the wrong padding/text-brightness for the content type (kb-card body is primary-statement-styled; finding-card body is supplemental-styled — correct for items in a list)

**Current violators in the suite** (May 30, 2026):
- `ch4-health-h3` "Toddler Injury Prevention" (4 hazard categories: Bodily harm / Drowning / Burns / Falls)
- `ch20-hf-h1` "HF Medications" (4 drug classes: Digoxin / ACE inhibitors / Beta-blockers / Diuretics)
- `ch20-hf-h2` "HF Nursing care" (4 priorities: Conserve energy / Optimize oxygenation / Support nutrition / Monitor & support)
- `ch42-substance-h0` "NAS scoring" (3 body systems: CNS / Metabolic-vasomotor-respiratory / GI)

All 4 in PD Book. Each refactor is mechanical:
1. Replace `<div class="kb-card"><span class="kb-tag">...</span><h4>...</h4><ul>` with `<div class="finding-grid">`
2. Replace `</ul></div>` close with `</div>` close on finding-grid
3. Wrap each `<li>` in `<div class="finding-card"><h4>{Original bold keyword}</h4><ul><li>...</li></ul></div>`
4. Content unchanged; only wrapper structure changes

Estimated time per pill: ~2 minutes. Total refactor effort: ~10 minutes for all 4.

#### 34.10.4 — Inventing new classes (GENERAL FORBIDDEN PRACTICE)

**Rule:** Do not use any class name not defined in the CSS file of the book you're editing.

**Why forbidden:** The CSS file is the source of truth. Class names without a CSS rule render as completely unstyled — applying them creates no visual treatment. The result is identical to using no class at all, but the markup IMPLIES a treatment that isn't there. This:
- Misleads future authors who see the class name and assume it means something
- Adds visual inconsistency (the imagined treatment doesn't appear)
- Makes future refactors harder (the invented classes look like canonical ones)

**How to verify before using a class:** Search the book's CSS section for `.{classname}` — if no rule matches, the class is invented. Either:
- Use a documented class instead (consult §34.4–§34.9 for the catalog)
- Add a new CSS rule first (NOT a recommended path; consult human review)
- Skip the class entirely (most common correct path)

**Examples of invented classes seen in the wild:**
- `kb-tag` (§34.10.2)
- Hypothetical examples: `warning-callout`, `highlight-box`, `important-note`, `red-text`, `big-header` — none of these exist in MN's CSS.

#### 34.10.5 — Misapplying modifier classes (SCOPE VIOLATION)

**Pattern:** Using a modifier class on an element outside its documented scope.

**Examples:**

| Misapplication | Reason it fails | Correct alternative |
|---|---|---|
| `<h4 class="flag">` inside `<div class="finding-card">` (in MN, possibly) | The current CSS selector `.condition-name.flag, .kb-card h3.flag, .kb-card h4.flag` does NOT include `.finding-card h4.flag`. Bar accent may not render. See §34.9.1 note for the CSS gap. | Verify visual on live site; if bar doesn't render, escalate as CSS fix |
| `<td class="score-0">` outside a `data-table` | The selector `.data-table .score-0` requires the cell to be inside a table; outside, no styling | Either move into a data-table or use a different color mechanism |
| `<span class="severity reassuring">` as a heading | `.severity` is inline-flex; using it as a primary heading produces wrong size/visual hierarchy | Use `<h4>` with appropriate color via `.flag` or directly |
| `<p class="flag-list">` | `flag-list` is for `<ul>` and `<ol>` — applying to `<p>` does nothing | Use `<p>` for a lead, follow with `<ul class="flag-list">` for the list |

**Rule:** Before applying a modifier, check what selector(s) target it in the CSS. If the parent element + modifier combination isn't in the selector, the modifier is misapplied.

#### 34.10.6 — Double-flagging (SIGNAL DILUTION)

**Pattern:** Applying `.flag` (or warning treatment generally) in MULTIPLE locations within one pill.

**Example:**

```html
<!-- DOUBLE-FLAGGED — DO NOT DO THIS -->
<article class="condition-block">
  <header class="condition-head">
    <h3 class="condition-name flag">Postpartum hemorrhage</h3>
  </header>
  <ul class="flag-list">
    <li>Heavy bleeding</li>
    <li>Pale skin</li>
  </ul>
</article>
```

**Why anti-pattern:** The flag accent (red-coral vertical bar) is a visual SIGNAL that says "this is warning content." Applying it twice in one pill dilutes the signal — the eye notices it once and habituates, so the second application carries less weight. Worse, if you flag the title AND the list, future authors may add a flag tag too, accumulating to a noisy "shouting" pill.

**Rule:** Pick ONE flag location per pill. Choices in priority order:
1. `<ul class="flag-list">` for the body (when content IS a warning list)
2. `<h3 class="condition-name flag">` for the title (when the whole pill is about a warning concept)
3. `<span class="condition-tag flag">` for the header tag (when the warning is contextual to a non-warning topic)
4. `<h4 class="flag">` inside a finding-card or kb-card (when ONE sub-section is the warning)

**Choosing among them:** Use the location that most precisely localizes the warning. If the entire pill is a warning, flag the title. If only one section, flag that section's heading. Avoid the temptation to "amplify" by flagging multiple places.

#### 34.10.7 — Mixing `.flag` and `.severity` on same content (SYSTEM CONFUSION)

**Pattern:** Using both the binary `.flag` modifier and the graded `.severity` badge on the same content element.

**Why anti-pattern:** `.flag` and `.severity` are different signal systems:
- `.flag` = binary: warning vs not
- `.severity` = graded: reassuring vs concerning vs critical

Combining them creates ambiguity. Is the content "warning, graded concerning"? "Warning AND reassuring"? The semantics collide.

**Rule:** Use `.severity` for content where the 3-level scale is the meaning (FHR patterns, vital sign categorization, lab value classification). Use `.flag` for binary warning content with no graded scale. Never both.

#### 34.10.8 — Skipping the decision table (RECIPE-BY-TASTE)

**Pattern:** Choosing a pill body structure based on "this looks like it would work" rather than matching the content shape to §34.7.10.

**Why anti-pattern:** Without the decision table, recipe choice is subjective. The Batch E mistake (§34.10.3) is exactly this: I chose `kb-card` because it "looked like a good container" rather than checking the master decision table, which would have directed to `finding-grid + finding-card` for 4 parallel categories.

**Rule:** When composing a new pill:
1. State the content shape in one phrase ("4 parallel hazard categories with bullets each").
2. Match it to a row in §34.7.10 (master decision table).
3. Use that recipe.
4. If two rows seem to fit, prefer the more frequent one (more canonical).
5. If NO row seems to fit, the content shape may need re-examination — consider splitting the content into multiple pills, or escalate for human review. DO NOT invent a new composition.

#### 34.10.9 — `.nclex-tag` on regular content pills (SCOPE OVERREACH)

**Pattern:** Adding `<span class="nclex-tag">NCLEX · ...</span>` to ordinary content pills (chapter findings, medication overviews, etc.).

**Why anti-pattern:** The NCLEX category badge is meaningful only on Answer Key / exemplar / NCLEX-prep pills (per §34.6.2 and §34.7.8). Adding it to regular content pills:
- Treats the badge as decoration rather than meaningful metadata
- Diluts the badge's signal (when present, it should mean "this is exam prep" — not "this happens to be about a topic on the NCLEX")
- All MN content is broadly NCLEX-relevant; tagging every pill would defeat the purpose

**Rule:** `.nclex-tag` appears only on pills using Recipe 8 ("Answer Key Pattern" — §34.7.8). All 10 current MN usages follow this rule. Do not extend it.

#### 34.10.10 — Inventing new long-tail compositions (CANON DRIFT)

**Pattern:** Stacking pre-existing canonical blocks in a new combination not documented in §34.7.

**Why anti-pattern:** Even though each individual block is canonical, novel combinations introduce inconsistency. The 8 named recipes in §34.7 cover the content shapes MN actually has. If a content shape doesn't fit, the most likely explanation is that the shape was misclassified — not that a new recipe is needed.

**Existing long-tail compositions in MN (17 pills across 32 signatures):** Acknowledged in §34.7.9. These are PRE-EXISTING; not actively audited. Future-Claude should not ADD to the long tail without:
1. Documenting in a code comment why no named recipe fits
2. Recording the new signature in §34.7.9 if it becomes a recurring pattern
3. Consulting human review for content that genuinely needs novel structure

**Rule:** Default to named recipes (§34.7.1–§34.7.8). Long-tail variations are tolerated when pre-existing but not encouraged for new pills.

### 34.10.12 — When in doubt: escalate

If future-Claude encounters a content shape that genuinely doesn't fit any documented recipe AND can't be reframed to fit:

1. Document the situation in a comment in the source file (`<!-- LONG-TAIL: {content shape}; tried recipes A and B; neither fits because {reason}. Composing with {chosen structure} - needs review. -->`)
2. Use the closest matching recipe as a starting point, adjusted minimally
3. Add the new signature to a "needs review" log in Phase H (§34.12) for the next session

DO NOT silently invent a new pattern. Visibility into deviations is the only mechanism for keeping the canon coherent over time.


### 34.11 — Phase G: Decision tree (walk-through form)

The master decision table in §34.7.10 lets future-Claude look up a recipe when the content shape is known. This phase provides the same logic as a sequential walk-through — useful when shape classification is unclear and the right path emerges through guided yes/no questions.

**How to use this tree:**

1. Start at Q1 (root question).
2. Answer yes/no based on your content.
3. Follow the indicated branch.
4. Continue until you arrive at a leaf (a specific recipe number).
5. Open the linked recipe section for the skeleton and example pills.

If you end up at a leaf that doesn't match your content, return to the root and re-classify — most often the issue is a misread of the content's natural shape, not a gap in the tree.

---

**Q1 — Is the entire pill content ONE short statement (referral, single contraindication, single key teaching, one important callout)?**

- **YES** → Go to Q1a
- **NO** → Go to Q2

  **Q1a — Does the statement need a brief lead sentence before it to provide context (typically because the title alone isn't enough)?**

  - **YES** → **Recipe 6 (p + kb-card)** — §34.7.6 — 8 pills in MN
  - **NO** → **Single block: `<div class="kb-card">` alone** — §34.4.3 — 34 pills in MN

---

**Q2 — Is the entire pill content multiple INDEPENDENT primary statements (each warranting its own emphatic box, not parallel categories)?**

The distinguishing test: "Could these be presented as parallel sub-headings — Cause vs Symptom vs Treatment, or A vs B vs C?" If yes → they're categories (continue to Q3 path). If they're each standalone with no parallel relationship → stacked callouts.

- **YES** → **Recipe 7 (stacked kb-cards)** — §34.7.7 — 4-6 pills in MN
- **NO** → Go to Q3

---

**Q3 — Is the pill specifically an Answer Key / exemplar / NCLEX-prep pill (has the structure: opening concept rationale + practical applications + NCLEX category tag)?**

- **YES** → **Recipe 8 (Answer Key Pattern: kb-card + finding-grid + nclex-tag)** — §34.7.8 — 6 pills in MN. Note: this is the ONLY context for `<span class="nclex-tag">`; see §34.10.9.
- **NO** → Go to Q4

---

**Q4 — Is the content best expressed as a side-by-side COMPARISON across rows and columns (where the row-column relationship carries meaning that would be lost as a flat list)?**

- **YES** → **Single block: `<table class="data-table">`** — §34.6.1 — 6 pills in MN
- **NO** → Go to Q5

---

**Q5 — Does the content naturally divide into 2-6 PARALLEL CATEGORIES of equal weight (where each category would naturally take its own sub-heading, e.g., 4 drug classes / 4 hazard types / 3 body systems / 2-6 treatment options)?**

- **YES** → Go to Q5a (categories path)
- **NO** → Go to Q6 (flat list path)

  **Q5a — Does the categories breakdown need a brief lead sentence (one or two sentences) framing the topic?**

  - **YES** → Go to Q5b
  - **NO** → Go to Q5c

    **Q5b — Does the breakdown end with a wrap-up note that applies to ALL categories (e.g., a contraindication, a key teaching, a summary reminder)?**

    - **YES** → **Recipe 4 / Deluxe (p + finding-grid + kb-card)** — §34.7.4 — 17 pills in MN
    - **NO** → **Recipe 1 (p + finding-grid)** — §34.7.1 — 43 pills in MN

    **Q5c — Does the breakdown end with a wrap-up note (applying to all categories)?**

    - **YES** → **Recipe 3 (finding-grid + kb-card)** — §34.7.3 — 17 pills in MN
    - **NO** → **Single block: `<div class="finding-grid">` alone** — §34.4.1 — 160 pills in MN. (Most common multi-card pattern.)

---

**Q6 — The content is a flat list of items (no parallel categories). Continue: is the entire list WARNING content (red flags, reportable signs, "report immediately" criteria)?**

- **YES** → Go to Q6a (warning list path)
- **NO** → Go to Q7 (regular list path)

  **Q6a — Does the warning content have SEQUENCE (procedural priority — "first do X, then Y, then Z")?**

  - **YES** → **Single block: `<ol class="flag-list">`** — §34.6.3 — 1 pill in MN (extremely rare)
  - **NO** → **Single block: `<ul class="flag-list">` alone** — §34.5.3 — 37 pills in MN. Pair with `<span class="condition-tag flag">Red flags</span>` in the header by convention.

---

**Q7 — The content is a regular (non-warning) flat list. Continue: does the list have SEQUENCE (procedural steps in order)?**

- **YES** → Go to Q7a
- **NO** → Go to Q8

  **Q7a — Does the procedure need a brief lead sentence?**

  - **YES** → Long-tail composition: `p + ol`. Acceptable if content genuinely needs a lead before a numbered procedure; very rare in MN (1-2 pills). Document in a code comment per §34.10.10.
  - **NO** → **Single block: `<ol>` alone** — §34.5.2 — 4 pills in MN

---

**Q8 — The content is a regular flat bulleted list. Does it need a brief lead sentence?**

- **YES** → Go to Q8a
- **NO** → Go to Q9

  **Q8a — Does the list end with a wrap-up note?**

  - **YES** → Long-tail composition: `p + ul + kb-card`. 2 pills in MN. Document why no named recipe fits.
  - **NO** → **Recipe 2 (p + ul)** — §34.7.2 — 22 pills in MN

---

**Q9 — The content is a flat bulleted list with no lead needed. Does the list end with a wrap-up note?**

- **YES** → **Recipe 5 (ul + kb-card)** — §34.7.5 — 13 pills in MN
- **NO** → **Single block: `<ul>` alone** — §34.5.1 — **172 pills in MN — the single most common pattern.**

---

### 34.11.1 — Tree summary (compact)

Compact form of the same tree for quick reference (each arrow = "if yes":

```
START: New pill needed
├── Q1 (one short statement?) → kb-card or p+kb-card
├── Q2 (multiple INDEPENDENT primary statements, not parallel?) → kb-card+kb-card stack
├── Q3 (Answer Key / NCLEX-prep pill?) → kb-card+finding-grid+nclex-tag
├── Q4 (row-column comparison data?) → table.data-table
├── Q5 (2-6 parallel categories?)
│     ├── Q5a (needs lead?)
│     │     ├── Q5b (also needs closer?)
│     │     │     ├── YES → p+finding-grid+kb-card (Deluxe)
│     │     │     └── NO  → p+finding-grid
│     │     └── Q5c (needs closer, no lead?)
│     │           ├── YES → finding-grid+kb-card
│     │           └── NO  → finding-grid alone
├── Q6 (warning list?)
│     ├── Q6a (warning sequence?) → ol.flag-list (rare)
│     └── NO seq → ul.flag-list
├── Q7 (procedural sequence, non-warning?)
│     ├── Q7a (needs lead?) → p+ol (long tail)
│     └── NO lead → ol alone
├── Q8 (list with lead?)
│     ├── Q8a (also closer?) → p+ul+kb-card (long tail)
│     └── NO closer → p+ul (Recipe 2)
└── Q9 (plain list, no lead?)
      ├── (with closer?) → ul+kb-card
      └── (no closer) → ul alone (MOST COMMON)
```

### 34.11.2 — Escape hatch for edge cases

If your content reaches a leaf that doesn't seem right, OR you can't confidently answer any question along the way:

1. **Re-classify the content shape.** Ask: "What is the simplest description of this content?" The shape often emerges from the description. ("A list of warnings about postpartum hemorrhage" → flat list, warning → `ul.flag-list`.)
2. **Consider splitting.** If content seems to need multiple recipes at once, it may be two separate pills wearing one title. Split.
3. **Default to the most common pattern.** When in doubt between two close options, prefer the more frequent one (more canonical).
4. **Long-tail with documentation.** If genuinely novel, use the closest fit + document in a code comment + log for review (§34.10.12).
5. **Escalate.** Some content genuinely needs human review of canon scope. Note it and move on.

### 34.11.3 — Decision tree as workflow guide

For future-Claude composing a new pill, the recommended workflow is:

1. **Read the source content** carefully — what does it say?
2. **Classify the shape** by answering Q1-Q9 in this tree.
3. **Look up the recipe** in §34.4-§34.7 using the leaf result.
4. **Copy the skeleton** from the recipe section.
5. **Fill in `{placeholders}`** with source-faithful content.
6. **Verify against the example pills** named in the recipe — spot-check one on the live site.
7. **Run the validation rules** in §34.10 (forbidden patterns) before finalizing.

This sequence converts content authoring from an ambiguous design choice into a deterministic pipeline. Each step has a clear input and output.

#### 34.12.5 — Future-author guidance: how to USE PART 34

For a future-Claude opening PART 34 for the first time (or a returning Claude in a new session):

**Recommended reading order:**

1. **§34.1** — Why this catalog exists (rationale + the Batch E mistake that prompted it)
2. **§34.10** — Forbidden patterns (what NOT to do, with the refactor catalog of currently-violating pills)
3. **§34.11** — Decision tree (the walk-through for picking a recipe)
4. **§34.7.10** — Master decision table (the lookup version)
5. **§34.4 – §34.7** — Building blocks and composition recipes (skeletons + CSS + when-to-use)
6. **§34.8** — Pill shell conventions (the outer wrapper that every pill shares)
7. **§34.9** — Modifier classes (the small treatments layered on blocks)

**Recommended workflow for composing a new pill:**

1. Read source content carefully.
2. Run §34.11 decision tree → arrive at a recipe.
3. Open the recipe section (§34.4-§34.7).
4. Copy the skeleton, fill in `{placeholders}` with source-faithful content.
5. Verify against the recipe's example pill IDs (spot-check one on live site).
6. Validate against §34.10 forbidden patterns.
7. Apply.

**Recommended workflow for refactoring an existing pill:**

1. Read the pill on live site or in source file — identify the current pattern.
2. Cross-reference §34.10.11 (refactor catalog) — is this pill in there?
   - YES → use the documented target structure
   - NO → run §34.11 decision tree against the content shape; if the result differs from current pattern, refactor accordingly
3. Apply the refactor per §34.10.11 mechanical steps.
4. Verify the new render matches the recipe's example pills.

**Recommended workflow when content doesn't fit any recipe:**

1. Re-classify the content shape (most often the issue is mis-reading, not a gap).
2. Consider splitting the pill into two pills.
3. Use the closest fit + document the decision in a code comment.
4. Log for human review.
5. NEVER silently invent a new pattern. See §34.10.12 (escalation rule).

## PART 35 — PHARM FLASHCARDS AUDIT PROTOCOL [v1.0]

### 35.1 — Why audit

The Pharm Flashcards deck started this audit era with **644 cards** anchored to all 49 chapters (full coverage breadth). However, depth analysis revealed:

- **249 of 644 cards** under 200 chars — many are appropriately atomic for their content, but a meaningful subset compress multiple facts into single short answers
- **Variable depth across the deck** — some cards 100 chars (calc problems, appropriate), some 1000+ chars (multi-topic concept cards, NOT appropriate)
- **Spaced repetition concern**: cards testing multiple facts in one Q/A violate the **minimum information principle** (Wozniak, SuperMemo) — the foundational tenet of effective SRS

The audit's purpose is to bring every chapter to a consistent quality bar where each card tests **one atomic fact** — improving the deck's effectiveness as a study tool while preserving the existing coverage.

### 35.2 — Why SPLIT, not ENRICH (the design decision)

**Initial proposal (rejected May 31, 2026):** Enrich short cards by expanding answers from ~200 chars to ~500 chars with mechanism + monitoring + clinical implications all in one card.

**Why this was wrong:** It violated the atomic principle. A 500-char card with 5 facts produces:
- Ambiguous self-grading (got 3 of 5 right — pass or fail?)
- Cross-contamination (forgetting one sub-fact reschedules the whole card)
- Increased cognitive load per review
- Encoding asymmetry (Q tests one thing, A covers five)

**Correct approach (SPLIT):** Keep the existing short card as-is, ADD new atomic companion cards covering the related facts as separate Q/A pairs. The deck grows; each card stays SRS-optimal.

**Worked example (from this session — fc-ch3-furosemide-push):**

```
ORIGINAL CARD (kept):
  Q: Max IV push rate for furosemide, and why?
  A: ≤ 20 mg/min. Pushing faster risks ototoxicity (hearing loss).

ADDED ATOMIC COMPANIONS:
  • fc-ch3-furosemide-ototox — manifestations to monitor
  • fc-ch3-furosemide-lytes — electrolyte abnormalities
  • fc-ch3-furosemide-onset — expected diuretic onset timing
```

Result: 1 topic now has 4 atomic cards instead of 1 enriched card. Each tests one thing.

**Future Claude MUST follow SPLIT, not ENRICH.** This decision is final unless materially new SRS research changes the consensus.

### 35.3 — The audit protocol (per-chapter workflow)

For each chapter, the workflow is:

**Step 1: Survey (~10 min)**

- Open the Pharm Book chapter (HTML) and list all pills (`<article class="condition-block">`)
- Filter STARTER_DECK for cards where `ch === '{chapter_id}'`
- Map each card's anchor to a Book pill (or chapter-level concept)

**Step 2: Identify gaps (~10 min)**

Ask three questions per chapter:

1. **Coverage check:** does every Book pill have at least one anchored flashcard? (Note: existing anchoring is chapter-level not pill-level — if pill-level anchoring is added later, this check will be sharper)
2. **Atomicity check:** for each existing card, count distinct testable facts in the answer. >1 = candidate for splitting.
3. **Drug-specificity check:** for each drug named in the chapter, is there a card covering each of: mechanism, monitoring, adverse effects, contraindications, patient teaching? Missing aspects = candidate for new atomic cards.

**Step 3: Draft new atomic cards (~15-25 min per chapter)**

- For each gap, draft a Q/A pair under 250 chars
- Follow naming convention: `fc-{ch}-{drug-or-topic}-{aspect}` (e.g., `fc-ch3-furosemide-ototox`)
- Use the same JS object format as existing cards (id, ch, type, anchor, q, a)
- Match drug-specific source content from Pharm ATI PDF
- Use `type: 'warning'` for safety-critical facts, `type: 'concept'` for general teaching, `type: 'priority'` for ABCs/critical assessments, `type: 'calc'` for math problems

**Step 4: User check-in (varies)**

- Present new cards in a table (id / type / Q / A / char count)
- Get approval as a batch or per-card (user preference)

**Step 5: Apply + verify (~5 min)**

- Use `str_replace` to insert new cards into STARTER_DECK array after their parent card
- Verify deck integrity (parse all cards, confirm count delta matches expected, confirm no JS syntax errors)
- Confirm `updateStarterCount()` will auto-sync UI (no manual UI update needed — see §35.7)

### 35.4 — Quality bar — what "audited" means

A chapter is marked **audited** when ALL of these are true:

| Criterion | Standard | How to verify |
|---|---|---|
| **Coverage** | Every important Book topic has ≥1 flashcard | Map cards to Book topics; no orphan topics |
| **Atomicity** | No card tests more than 2 closely-related facts | Read each answer; count distinct testable claims |
| **Length** | All answers under ~250 chars | `len(answer)` check programmatically |
| **Source fidelity** | All content traces to Pharm Book / Pharm ATI PDF | Spot-check sourcing during draft phase |
| **Anchoring** | All cards anchored | Check `anchor` field non-empty (currently 100%) |
| **Naming** | Card IDs follow `fc-{ch}-{topic}-{aspect}` | Naming convention check |

Chapters that fail any criterion get noted in §35.5 progress tracker as "needs follow-up."

### 35.6 — Hand-off notes for mid-stream audit work

When future-Claude resumes audit work mid-stream:

1. **Identify the boundary** — open the §35.5 progress tracker; find the most recent "audited" chapter
2. **Verify file state** — programmatically count cards per chapter; confirm match with tracker
3. **Resume from the next "pending" chapter** in the tracker
4. **Update the tracker** after each chapter completes (chapter row + date + cards added + notes)

If a chapter is marked "partial-audit," it means atomic companion cards were added for SOME topics in that chapter but the full audit (coverage check + all-drug-coverage) wasn't done. Full audit reviews ALL pills in the chapter against ALL flashcards.

### 35.7 — Infrastructure baseline (as of audit kick-off)

The Pharm Flashcards file `Elevated ATI Pharm Flashcards.html` has the following infrastructure:

- **STARTER_DECK array** at position ~39,776 chars into file — flat JS array of card objects
- **Each card** has fields: `id`, `ch`, `type`, `anchor`, `q`, `a`
- **Card types** in use: `warning` (321), `concept` (283), `priority` (33), `calc` (7)
- **Hardcoded UI count** removed in 2026-05-31 session; replaced with `updateStarterCount()` IIFE function that auto-syncs button text + tooltip with `STARTER_DECK.length` on every page load
- **Anchor format** is chapter-level (e.g., `ch3-tldr`, `ch1-absorption`) — NOT pill-level. Future enhancement: pill-level anchoring would enable sharper Book↔Flashcard linking but requires significant data work.

When adding new cards, no UI updates needed — the dynamic counter handles it automatically.

### 35.8 — Decision log (lessons learned during audit kick-off)

1. **SPLIT, not ENRICH.** See §35.2 for rationale. Final decision May 31, 2026.
2. **Per-chapter batches** with user check-ins. Not per-card check-ins (too slow at the 16-session scale) and not bulk all-chapter check-ins (too risky for content authoring quality).
3. **Chronological order.** Simplest tracking, ensures complete coverage, builds confidence with foundations before complex pharmacology.
4. **Quality bar in §35.4 is the contract.** Don't lower it for convenience.
5. **Hardcoded UI counts are anti-pattern.** Future card additions should use `STARTER_DECK.length` dynamically — never hardcode counts in HTML. This is now infrastructure (§35.7).

## PART 36 — CROSS-CHAPTER NAVIGATION FEATURE [v1.0]

### 36.1 — Why this feature exists

The Books use **modal-based chapter navigation** — only one chapter's content is visible at a time (in the active modal). All other chapters' HTML exists in the document but is hidden via `.chapter-pool { display: none }`.

Native browser anchor navigation (`<a href="#some-id">`) **does not work** with this architecture, because the target element exists but is inside hidden content. The browser can't scroll to it, so the click silently fails.

This was discovered May 31, 2026 when a user clicked the only cross-chapter link in the suite (`#ch9-magsulfate` in `ch10-tocolytics-cb1` of the MN Book) and nothing happened.

### 36.2 — How the feature works

A JavaScript click handler intercepts all clicks on anchor links matching `<a href="#ch{N}...">`. Instead of letting the browser try to scroll, it:

1. Parses the chapter ID from the href (e.g., `#ch9-magsulfate` → chapter = `ch9`)
2. Verifies the chapter exists in `.chapter-pool`
3. If a modal is already open, closes it first
4. Calls `openChapter(chapterId, fullTargetId)` to open the target chapter modal
5. The `openChapter` function uses `fullTargetId` to activate the matching tab (if `fullTargetId` matches a section ID)
6. After modal opens, if the target is a pill (not a section/tab), scrolls to it within the modal body

### 36.3 — Supported anchor formats

| Href format | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `#ch{N}` (e.g., `#ch9`) | Opens chapter, first section active |
| `#ch{N}-{section}` (e.g., `#ch9-magsulfate`) | Opens chapter, that section's tab active |
| `#ch{N}-{section}-{cb#}` (e.g., `#ch7-placenta-previa-cb0`) | Opens chapter, parent section's tab active, then scrolls to the pill within the modal |

### 36.4 — Where the handler lives

In all 4 Books, the handler is placed immediately after the `closeChapterModal()` function definition, before the `modalClose.addEventListener` line. The handler is identical across all 4 books (suite-wide consistency).

### 36.5 — When to use cross-chapter links

Cross-chapter `<a href="#ch{N}-...">` links should be used sparingly — only when the cross-reference adds significant clinical value (e.g., pointing to a drug's critical reference section when the drug is mentioned in passing in another chapter).

Currently 1 cross-chapter link exists in the suite (MN Ch 10 → MN Ch 9 magsulfate reference). Future authors can add more, knowing the navigation will work correctly.

### 36.6 — Limitations and future enhancements

- **In-modal anchors:** Anchor links WITHIN the currently-open chapter modal don't go through this handler. They use the browser's native scroll. This works because the in-modal content IS visible. (The handler only intercepts links that look like cross-chapter — starting with `#ch`.)
- **Browser history:** Cross-chapter clicks do NOT push to browser history. Back-button behavior is unaffected. Future enhancement could push state for back-button navigation.
- **Deep links from outside:** Direct URL navigation (typing `https://site.com/page.html#ch9-magsulfate` in the URL bar) is not yet supported. Future enhancement could read the URL hash on page load and call `openChapter` accordingly.

### 36.7 — Documenting cross-chapter links

When adding a new cross-chapter link, document it in a comment in the Build Guide §36.8 (the registry). Format: `{book} {source} → {target}` plus a brief reason.

### 36.8 — Cross-chapter link registry

Active cross-chapter links in the suite:

| Book | Source location | Target | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| MN | `ch10-tocolytics-cb1` Magnesium sulfate (as tocolytic) | `#ch9-magsulfate` (MN Ch 9 Magnesium Sulfate Critical Reference section) | The tocolytic pill is brief; the comprehensive magsulfate reference (toxicity signs, antidote, etc.) is in Ch 9 |

# PART 37 — Pharm Templates Enrichment Audit (v1.0)

**Status:** Active
**Started:** 2026-05-31
**Goal:** Enrich the Pharm Templates HTML file by adding chapter-specific ATI templates (Medication, System Disorder, Basic Concept, etc.) for major drugs/concepts that lack dedicated template coverage.

## 37.1 — Audit philosophy

Same as PART 35 (Flashcards audit):
- Per-chapter audit with check-in before applying
- Saturation rule: skip chapters where every major drug/concept already has a template
- Quality over quantity — templates take time to write properly (they are not 1-line entries)
- Track in §37.5 progress tracker

## 37.2 — Template types (ATI Active Learning Templates)

The Pharm Templates file uses 9 categories from the ATI ALS system:
1. **Basic Concept** — foundational pharmacology principles
2. **Diagnostic Procedure** — lab tests, drug level monitoring
3. **Growth and Development** — age-specific pharm (peds, geri)
4. **Medication** — drug-specific (most common type for Pharm)
5. **Nursing Skill** — procedural (e.g., insulin admin, IV push)
6. **System Disorder** — disease + meds (less common for pure Pharm)
7. **Therapeutic Procedure** — interventional (e.g., chemo, blood transfusion)
8. **Concept Analysis** — concept-mapping
9. **Worked Example** — already used for ALS section examples

## 37.3 — Current state (baseline 2026-05-31)

**File:** `Elevated ATI Pharm Templates.html`
**Existing examples:** 105 across 49 chapters
**Distribution:** Uneven — 23 chapters have only 1 example, 4 chapters have 4+ examples.

## 37.4 — Insertion methodology

- Each new example uses the same `<div class="example-card" data-mode="filled" id="ex-chN-{slug}">` pattern
- Header: example-label, example-name, example-source (with link to book chapter)
- Body: `template-meta` (Student Name, Procedure, Review Module Chapter) + `tp-grid` with appropriate `tp-box` sections per template type
- Use proper ATI template field labels per template type

System Disorder section correctly drops 11 → 8. No new content fabricated; no duplicate IDs. **Total examples unchanged at 249.**

**Badge-count sync (whole-file fix, post-audit):** Found that section status-badges were HARDCODED and stale across the entire file (e.g., medication badge said "93 examples" with 208 actual; basic-concept "1 examples" with 4 actual; also ungrammatical "1 examples"). Re-synced all 8 section badges to actual example counts with correct singular/plural: basic-concept 4, diagnostic-procedure 3, growth-development 3, medication 208, nursing-skill 12, system-disorder 8, therapeutic-procedure 8, concept-analysis 3. **NOTE for future: these badges are static text, not dynamically computed — adding examples requires manually updating the section badge, OR (better) a future enhancement should compute them from `.example-card` counts at load time (cf. the Flashcards `updateStarterCount()` dynamic pattern).**

**DYNAMIC BADGE AUTO-COUNT IMPLEMENTED (post-audit):** Added `syncSectionBadges()` to the existing print-button IIFE (last `<script>` block in `Elevated ATI Pharm Templates.html`). On load it iterates `section.template-section`, counts `.example-card` children, and rewrites each `.status-badge` text to `Active · N example(s)` (correct singular/plural) — or `Coming soon · 0 examples` + coming-soon class when empty. Called on DOMContentLoaded alongside `injectPrintButtons()`. The static badge text was ALSO corrected to match (so counts are right even with JS disabled — defensive double-coverage). Validated via `node --check` (syntax OK) and a DOM-mock simulation (all 8 sections: static == JS output). **Future example additions now auto-update section badges on load — no manual badge edits needed.** This is the Templates-file analogue of the Flashcards `updateStarterCount()` pattern (per persistent rule: never hardcode UI counts).
